title: Reasoning Language (CRL)

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.html:
This document specifies CRL — the CHOIR Reasoning Language — as the human-facing surface syntax for MIR, giving its design constraints, an EBNF grammar, worked examples in three domains, a type system, an explicit list of what the language cannot express, and a formal semantics (§1–§8). It discharges a debt recorded in knowledge_graph_spec.md §4.3: choosing a hypergraph means CHOIR inherits no formal semantics and must supply its own (§7). The source carries the status "Draft for review" and records six open questions of its own, including that its primary design constraint — reviewability by non-programmers — is untested (§9).

Status note. This document is Active: it is a complete research document, drafted, and not accepted as specification. Per choir/research/README.md, every document in this series is a hypothesis — all 18 deliverables drafted, none accepted. Nothing below should be read as a governing ruling.

sections.heading: Research Question
sections.html:
The source frames its task in §1: CRL "is the human-facing surface syntax for MIR. It is what a scholar or domain expert reads when reviewing an extracted rule, and what they write when authoring one directly." The question is therefore what surface syntax makes the distinctions established in Phases 1–3 visible to a domain expert who is not a programmer, while remaining restricted enough "that termination is provable and every construct maps to a MIR node" (§1).

§7 states a second question the document sets out to answer, inherited as a debt: knowledge_graph_spec.md §4.3 "incurred a debt: choosing a hypergraph means CHOIR inherits no formal semantics and must supply its own. This section discharges it."

sections.heading: Finding
sections.html:
Design constraints and the deliberate cost of verbosity (§1)

The document states five design constraints, in priority order (§1):

  1. Reviewable by a domain expert who is not a programmer. "The primary reader is a Sanskritist, a lawyer, or a clinician."
  2. Lossless round-trip with MIR for accepted rules.
  3. No construct without a MIR counterpart. "The surface cannot express more than the IR."
  4. Distinctions that matter must be syntactically visible — exception type, reference frame, modality, completeness. "Anything left implicit will be got wrong."
  5. Confidence cannot be written. "There is no syntax for a confidence literal."

The source is explicit that CRL is "not a general-purpose logic programming language" (§1), and that constraint 4 is the reason for its verbosity: "UNDERCUT WHEN is longer than unless, and the length is the point: an author must state which kind of defeater this is" (§1).

Additions to the brief's shape (§2)

The research brief sketched WHEN … THEN … SUPPORTED_BY … EXCEPT …. CRL keeps that shape and adds seven constructs, each traced by the source to a prior phase (§2):

AdditionRequired by
WITHIN — context scopeContradiction tolerance (001 §3.10)
FROM — reference frameR10; apādāna (005 §6.4)
INDICATES / ASSERTS / OBLIGES … — modalityDeontic domains (001 §3.9)
UNDERCUT vs REBUT vs DENYDefeater typology (001 §3.12)
COMPLETENESSException completeness (007 §2.1)
ABSENT … ASSUMING COMPLETEanupalabdhi observability (009 §3.3)
CONFIDENCE DERIVEDConfidence is computed (011 §1)

Grammar and the syntactic choices it encodes (§3, §3.1)

§3 gives a full EBNF grammar for RULE declarations: optional VERSION, SOURCE, WITHIN, GIVEN and REQUIRES clauses; a WHEN condition; one or more THEN conclusions; an optional EXCEPT block; an optional SUPPORTED_BY; and a mandatory CONFIDENCE DERIVED before END. Conditions admit AND, OR, NOT, parenthesisation, ANY n OF (…), ABSENT (…) ASSUMING COMPLETE <ident>, and FOR ALL / EXISTS quantification over a domain. Modality is one of INDICATES, ASSERTS, OBLIGES, PERMITS, FORBIDS, REQUIRES_THAT; STRENGTH is admitted "only if the source states it". Defeaters are UNDERCUT WHEN, REBUT WHEN … ASSERTING <proposition>, or DENY WHEN, with COMPLETENESS one of KNOWN, LIKELY_INCOMPLETE, UNKNOWN.

§3.1 records four choices and their rationale:

  • REBUT … ASSERTING <proposition> requires the proposition. "A rebutting defeater must state what it concludes instead… if the author cannot name the opposite conclusion, the defeater is undercutting." Because undercutting is "the śāstric default" (shloka_compiler.md §6.3), the source holds that "making rebutting the syntactically expensive option is the right bias."
  • FROM is a clause on the atom, not an argument. "It corresponds to a distinct kāraka and must remain visible in explanations." Writing house_of(G) FROM M rather than house_from(G, M) keeps the reference frame syntactically marked.
  • ABSENT(...) ASSUMING COMPLETE <domain> makes the observability condition unavoidable, "enforcing evidence_model.md §3.3 at the syntax level rather than by review."
  • CONFIDENCE DERIVED is mandatory boilerplate. "It exists to make the absence of a confidence literal conspicuous."

Worked examples (§4)

The benchmark rule (§4.1). The Gajakesari formation is written with SOURCE unverified and the inline annotation -- E-ATTEST: blocks acceptance; WITHIN application = jātaka, chart = rāśi (both marked inherited, prakaraṇa); GIVEN G : Graha = Guru, M : Graha = Candra; WHEN house_of(G) FROM M IN kendra; THEN INDICATES forms(Gajakesari) NAMED Gajakesari, with the comment "no STRENGTH clause: the source states none"; three UNDERCUT WHEN defeaters (debilitated, combust, afflicted) and COMPLETENESS UNKNOWN. The source compares this against a naive encoding (if jupiter_in_kendra_from_moon and not debilitated: yoga = True) and states that the naive version "loses the modality, the reference frame's grammatical status, the exception typing, the completeness qualification, the context scope, and the source — six distinctions that Phases 1–3 established as load-bearing" (§4.1).

Influence as a separate declaration (§4.2). INFLUENCE has TARGETS, WHEN, EFFECT and SOURCE clauses but "no THEN clause. It is syntactically incapable of asserting a conclusion, which enforces computational_primitives.md §3.7 in the grammar rather than by convention."

ANY n OF (§4.3). The source justifies the construct on explanation grounds: expanded to disjunctive normal form, ANY 3 OF five conditions "is ten conjunctions, and the explanation would say 'one of ten alternative condition sets was met' rather than 'three of five criteria were satisfied, namely a, c and d.' The threshold structure is what the reader needs."

Cross-domain (§4.4). A legal rule (limitation_bar, sourced to "Limitation Act": "s.5" ED "2023 consolidation") and a clinical rule (renal_dose_reduction) are written in the same grammar. The source concludes: "Three domains, one grammar, zero core changes… both are modality values, not new syntax. domain_independence.md §6 measures exactly this." It also notes that the legal rule "uses all three defeater types — a disability provision denies a premise, an acknowledgement provision rebuts with an explicit opposite conclusion, and the distinction between them is legally significant."

One textual point is worth recording for a reader checking the grammar against the examples: §4.4 states that the clinical example's RECOMMENDS is a modality value; the modality production given in §3 enumerates INDICATES, ASSERTS, OBLIGES, PERMITS, FORBIDS, REQUIRES_THAT, and RECOMMENDS does not appear in that enumeration. The source does not comment on the difference.

Type system (§5)

Types are Entity and its subtypes (from L1, refined by L2), Proposition, Ordinal ("Ranked; arithmetic prohibited"), Measure (value + unit + scale type), Interval (temporal), and the reference types ContextRef, SourceRef, RuleRef. Type checking is against the ontology (reasoning_ontology.md) and the source lists six errors it catches: predicate applied to the wrong entity type; a reference frame that is not a valid frame entity; arithmetic on an ordinal (the Measure.scale_type check); a defeater whose stratum does not decrease; a rebutting defeater without an asserted proposition; and absence without a completeness declaration. The last two are caught by the grammar, not the type checker, and the source states this is deliberate: "they are the distinctions most often elided, so they are made unwriteable rather than merely invalid" (§5).

What CRL deliberately cannot express (§6)

Not expressibleWhy
A confidence literalConfidence is derived (011 §1)
A strength not in the sourceNumber invention (007 §5.4)
Untyped defeatType must be stated
Absence without completenessObservability condition (009 §3.3)
Context-free rulesEvery rule needs a scope (WITHIN may be empty but must be considered)
Function symbols / term constructionTermination (§7.3)
Unrestricted recursionTermination (§7.3)
Side effectsReplay guarantee (012 §4.1)
An influence with a conclusionInfluence is second-order (001 §3.7)

"A language is defined as much by what it forbids as by what it permits. Each row here corresponds to a failure mode identified in Phases 1–3" (§6).

Semantics (§7)

Two layers (§7.1), mirroring evidence_model.md §5.1. Layer 1 is structural: rules and defeaters induce an argumentation framework in which arguments are inference instances and attacks are defeater relations, with each argument labelled in, out, or undecided. Undercutting defeat "removes the inference, not the conclusion"; rebutting defeat "is a symmetric attack between conclusions"; premise defeat "removes an argument's support"; and "undecided is a real output and is what surfaces as vikalpa" (conflict_resolution.md §7.1). Grounded (sceptical) labelling is the default — "an argument is in only if all its attackers are out" — described as "the conservative choice… where the cost of asserting a defeated conclusion exceeds the cost of withholding one." Layer 2 is graded: "Only in arguments proceed to confidence computation… Defeat is never a weight."

Non-monotonicity (§7.2). "Adding a rule can retract a conclusion. This is intended: it is what apavāda means." Consequences recorded: conclusions are stamped with the corpus version that produced them; adding rules triggers re-evaluation of dependents via derives_from; historical conclusions remain replayable under their original version (reasoning_ontology.md §7.3).

Termination (§7.3) is guaranteed by four restrictions — no function symbols (so the Herbrand universe is finite); finite domains for quantifiers; stratification, with recursion within a stratum prohibited and strata derivable from the corpus's hierarchical structure (vedic_reasoning_methodology.md §5.2); and well-founded defeat, attack strata strictly decreasing (choir_intermediate_representation.md IR7). "Together: evaluation reaches a fixpoint in bounded steps, and the bound is computable from the corpus." Where a bound is hit — a truncated defeater chain — "the system reports it rather than returning a result as though analysis completed" (conflict_resolution.md §6, explainability_framework.md §2.2).

Context semantics (§7.4) is unresolved. Whether a rule scoped to context c also sees facts from more general contexts (lattice-upward closure) "remains open" (knowledge_graph_spec.md §8.2). Two readings are recorded:

ReadingEffect
Closed — only exact contextPredictable; may miss genuinely applicable general facts
Upward-closed — inherits from more general contextsNatural; risks importing facts that do not hold in the specific context

"Per MANIFESTO.md, both are recorded rather than collapsed. The current inclination is closed by default, with explicit INHERITS opt-in, because silent inheritance is exactly the anuvṛtti failure mode (sanskrit_analysis_pipeline.md §7) reappearing at execution time" (§7.4). The source records this as an inclination, not a decision.

Tooling requirements (§8)

Seven capabilities are listed: round-trip check MIR ↔ CRL (constraint 2); type check against the ontology (§5); stratification check (§7.3); well-foundedness check (IR7); diff two rule versions (supersession review); render with source alongside (scholar review, canonical_shloka_analysis.md); and multi-script identifiers, IAST and Devanāgarī (reasoning_ontology.md §7.1). On the last: "Identifiers must accept Devanāgarī and IAST as display forms over stable opaque identifiers, so a Sanskritist reads guru and a lawyer reads jyotisha:graha/Guru for the same object" (§8).

sections.heading: Architectural Implications
sections.html:
• The surface cannot outrun the IR. Constraint 3 fixes CRL as strictly no more expressive than MIR, and constraint 2 requires lossless round-trip for accepted rules (§1). Any MIR change that adds a node kind is a prerequisite for the corresponding CRL construct, not a consequence of one.
  • Certain errors are made unwriteable rather than merely invalid. Rebutting without an asserted proposition, and absence without a completeness declaration, are grammar errors by design (§3.1, §5). This moves enforcement of evidence_model.md §3.3 and the defeater typology out of review and into parsing.
  • Confidence is structurally excluded from authoring. There is no confidence literal, and CONFIDENCE DERIVED is mandatory boilerplate (§1, §3.1, §6). Confidence remains the responsibility of confidence_framework.md; defeat "is never a weight" (§7.1).
  • INFLUENCE is second-order by grammar. Having no THEN clause, it cannot assert a conclusion, enforcing computational_primitives.md §3.7 syntactically (§4.2).
  • Termination is bought by expressive restriction. No function symbols, finite domains, stratification, well-founded defeat (§7.3) — and §6 forbids function symbols and unrestricted recursion precisely to preserve this. Any future relaxation removes the computable bound.
  • Truncation is reported, not hidden. Hitting a bound surfaces as a reported condition rather than a completed analysis (§7.3), which is a requirement on conflict_resolution.md and explainability_framework.md.
  • undecided must be representable downstream. It is "a real output" surfacing as vikalpa (§7.1), so consumers of execution results cannot assume a two-valued answer.
  • Non-monotonicity imposes versioning obligations. Conclusions carry the corpus version; dependents are re-evaluated on rule addition; historical conclusions stay replayable (§7.2).
  • Domain independence is claimed and delegated for measurement. "Three domains, one grammar, zero core changes… domain_independence.md §6 measures exactly this" (§4.4) — the claim is asserted here and tested elsewhere.
  • Tooling is a precondition, not an accessory. The seven capabilities in §8, including multi-script identifiers over stable opaque identifiers, are stated as requirements for CRL to serve its intended readers.

sections.heading: Open Questions
sections.html:
The source records six open questions in §9, plus one unresolved item in §7.4:

  1. Is CRL genuinely reviewable by non-programmers? "Constraint 1 is the whole point and is untested. It needs trial with actual Sanskritists and lawyers, and the answer may force simplification that conflicts with constraint 4" (§9.1).
  2. Grounded vs preferred semantics. §7.1 chooses grounded (sceptical). "Preferred semantics would return more conclusions with less certainty. The choice interacts with how often vikalpa is produced, which is unmeasured" (§9.2).
  3. Context closure. "§7.4 is unresolved and materially affects both results and performance" (§9.3). §7.4 records an inclination — closed by default with explicit INHERITS opt-in — but not a decision.
  4. Should INFLUENCE be part of RULE? "Separating it emphasises second-order status but scatters related content across declarations" (§9.4).
  5. Deontic depth. "OBLIGES / PERMITS / FORBIDS are modality tags, not a full deontic logic. Whether obligations need proper deontic semantics — contrary-to-duty conditionals, for instance — is unexamined and matters for law" (§9.5).
  6. Temporal operators. "Only interval predicates are supported. Rules of the form 'within 30 days of X' are expressible via Derived kernels, which hides the temporal structure from the reasoner" (§9.6).

The benchmark rule in §4.1 additionally carries SOURCE unverified with the annotation -- E-ATTEST: blocks acceptance, and COMPLETENESS UNKNOWN; the INFLUENCE example in §4.2 is likewise SOURCE unverified.
